title: POC scoping: Stratus AI pilot - compliance, load & benchmarks
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a scoping call with Stratus AI to define pilot success criteria, security/compliance guardrails (SOC 2, ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logging, KMS), target throughput/latency for benchmarks, and an initial 6-week pilot timeline. Customer wants private control plane with VPC peering, sample SLA targets, and clear rollback/fallback behavior. Next steps: share security packet, draft benchmark harness, schedule lab run and follow-up meeting in 1 week.
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC 2 and ISO-27001 summary + security packet (Maya) - due 2025-12-15
SE to draft benchmark harness with sample queries and tokenization guidance (Owen) - due 2025-12-18
Customer to share sample workload (5000 queries/day and 200 concurrent users) and data residency constraints (Daniel) - due 2025-12-16
Schedule pilot kick-off lab and credentials exchange (calendar invite from Lena) - due 2025-12-19

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-12
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Owen (Redwood SE), Lena (CS), Daniel (Stratus Head of ML), Aisha (Stratus Security), Tom (Stratus Platform), Priya (Product)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya Chen, AE on the account. Owen is our SE who will run through sizing and benchmarks, and Lena will coordinate the pilot. 
[00:12] Daniel: Hi, thanks. I'll be driving the POC from our side, with Aisha for security and Tom for infra. Priya's on for product acceptance criteria.
[00:20] Owen: Great. Agenda — scope the pilot success criteria, understand the security constraints (SOC two, ISO twenty seven thousand, S S O M L — we heard SAML), sizing and expected load, and then a benchmark plan.
[00:32] Aisha: Quick callout — Stratus is regulated for financial summaries, so we need clear audit logs, key management, and proof of isolation for any PII. SOC two Type II and ISO 27001 are must-haves. We also prefer SSO via SAML and RBAC integration with our Okta directory.
[00:48] Maya: Understood. For the pilot we're proposing Redwood Private with a customer-controlled VPC peered to our control plane, or full on-prem for especially sensitive lanes. Would you be open to Private first?
[00:57] Daniel: Private sounds right. We want retention controls and the ability to disable logging of raw prompts if necessary. But we do need proofs for SOC two artifacts — like evidence of change control, access logs.
[01:10] Owen: On the logging side we can produce audit trails for every model call — token-level metadata, requestor identity, timestamps. There are config toggles to redact prompt text from stored logs; we can send hashes instead. Note: sometimes the transcription here says 'hashes' as 'ashes' in prior calls.
[01:26] Tom: Can you run through KMS options? We use AWS KMS with an internal key policy; we need to wrap keys and ensure HSM-backed keys for production.
[01:34] Owen: Yes — Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations. For Private we can bring your CMK, and the control plane stores only encrypted blobs. We also support HSM-backed keys for signing and for S3 encryption at rest. There can be some nuance with cross-account roles for the peering setup.
[01:52] Aisha: Ok. Also we need to understand the user access model. RBAC must map to Okta groups, with admin, dev, and viewer roles. And we need to record admin actions in audit logs for SOC two.
[02:10] Maya: That's standard. We expose an RBAC layer that syncs with SAML groups; admin actions are logged. For the pilot we can provision a handful of test roles.
[02:20] Priya: On success criteria — from product perspective we need answer quality parity with our existing hosted model (our internal baseline), latency under 400ms p95 for short prompts, and cost per 1k tokens within a target band. Also a reliable fallback path if a model variant trips a regression.
[02:36] Daniel: To add to that — we want reproducible benchmarks: throughput (QPS) and latency, cold vs warm cache, and memory/CPU footprint. We'll run a traffic pattern that resembles our peak: about 200 concurrent interactive users, 1,500 QPS burst across 10 clusters? sorry, I mean 1,500 QPS is peak across all regions — maybe I should explain the numbers: our day avg is ~5k requests/day but peak concurrency is tricky.
[02:58] Owen: Let's capture the concrete numbers now. Do you have a target sample: e.g., 2,000 total QPS trivial?
[03:05] Daniel: Sorry — correction — it's 5k requests/day, with peaks ~200 concurrent sessions, each session sending 1–2 requests per 30s. So target steady QPS is more like 20–30, but we need to sustain bursts hitting 200 concurrent.
[03:18] Owen: Good. For benchmarking we'll do both latency SLO tests and throughput stress tests. We'll set up a harness that uses your sample prompt set, with tokenization metrics. We'll also measure prefix cache hit rates and how batching affects p95 latency.
[03:32] Aisha: On data handling, we have a rule: anything flagged as PII must not be stored in logs nor in model training datasets. For the pilot we need a guarantee that no training occurs on customer prompts, and a signed attestation.
[03:45] Maya: Redwood policy: hosted models are not trained on customer data. For Private deployments, the runtime runs customer-only workloads; no training. We'll provide a written attestation and relevant policy excerpts.
[03:56] Tom: Network topology — we need VPC peering or PrivateLink; also egress to third-party telemetry must be blocked by default. Can Redwood accommodate that?
[04:04] Owen: Yes. Private supports VPC peering and restricted egress firewall rules. There's an initial setup step for peering and cross-account roles. We'll share the network diagram.
[04:15] Priya: What about failover? If Dedicated capacity is down, can requests fall back to a hosted model with obfuscated payloads? We want graceful degradation but keep data isolation guarantees.
[04:26] Owen: We support fallback policies, but for strict isolation customers often prefer capacity burst within their dedicated pools. Fallback to hosted is possible but you'd need to accept different data policies. For the pilot we can define a no-fallback mode to meet compliance.
[04:40] Aisha: If fallback is used, we need explicit approval and encryption of payloads at rest and in transit. And an audit of which requests used fallback.
[04:49] Maya: Noted.
[04:52] [05:00] Owen: Let's map the benchmark matrix:
- Baseline: your internal model latency and quality on 200 sample prompts.
- Latency SLO: p95 under 400ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens).
- Throughput: sustain 200 concurrent sessions with median latency under 250ms in warm cache scenario.
- Cold start: measure first-token latency for cold KV cache.
- Cost: estimate per-1k token cost and compare to your cost target.

[05:30] Daniel: For quality, we'll use BLEU-like automated metrics and a human evaluation on 100 samples.
[05:36] Owen: Great. We'll provide a benchmark harness that returns token counts, latencies, cache-hit ratios; we'll run both single-node and multi-node tests. We'll also run quantized model variants to show cost/latency trade-offs.
[05:50] Aisha: Regarding SOC 2 evidence: we will need change control logs, access provisioning evidence, encryption config exports, and incidental vendor risk assessments. Who from Redwood's side owns compiling that?
[06:02] Maya: I'll coordinate the security packet and provide SOC 2 summary, ISO-27001 scope, encryption controls, and a vendor risk questionnaire. We can also include recent penetration test summaries.
[06:12] Aisha: Great. Also need to verify retention settings — ability to set retention to 0 days for raw prompts.
[06:20] Owen: You can toggle retention at the workspace level; for Private we can set defaults to discard raw prompts and keep hashed references. We'll document the process and the logs you'll still receive (action-level logs without raw prompts).
[06:33] [06:40] Tom: On the infra side, what do you need from us for the lab run? VPC CIDRs? IAM roles? Test datasets?
[06:48] Owen: We need a VPC CIDR for peering, a cross-account role ARN for minimal setup, and a sample dataset with anonymized prompts. For load tests, a script or CSV of requests and expected tokens. If you can't share real data, synthetic-ish yet realistic traces are fine.
[07:02] Daniel: We'll redact PII. We'll also need an NDA addendum for the attestation docs.
[07:09] Maya: We can share the security packet under our NDA.
[07:12] [07:20] Priya: Timeline — what's realistic for a 6-week pilot? Kickoff + infra setup (week 1), benchmark harness and baseline tests (week 2–3), quality human eval and security artifact exchange (week 4), optimizations and second run (week 5), review and acceptance (week 6).
[07:34] Lena: That aligns with what we've done before. We'll aim to schedule the kickoff next Tuesday.
[07:40] Daniel: One more ask — for the acceptance criteria we want a regression alert system: if quality dips more than 5% vs baseline, auto rollback to previous model. Can Redwood do automatic rollbacks?
[07:52] Owen: Yes, rollout policies can include automatic rollback triggers tied to eval metrics. We'll include that in the pilot config. Note: for the lab we can simulate a regression to test rollback.
[08:04] Aisha: For SSO, we use Okta with SAML 2.0; MFA enforced. We'll need a test Okta SP metadata file.
[08:12] Maya: We'll provide SAML SP metadata and instructions for group mappings.
[08:17] [08:30] Owen: Quick note on cost modeling — we'll provide a simple calculator showing how batching, quantization, and cache TTL affect per-token spend. That will help Priya's cost target.
[08:42] Priya: Perfect.
[08:46] Daniel: Any blockers from Redwood side that would delay start?
[08:50] Owen: Nothing major. The only slight friction is network peering approval on your side; some security teams take a week to approve cross-account roles. We'll provide a hardened template to speed that.
[09:02] Maya: Recap of next steps: I'll send security docs and SOC 2 summary; Owen will deliver benchmark harness template; Lena will share kickoff calendar invite; Daniel will provide sample prompts and CIDR and Aisha will confirm the evidence list.
[09:18] Aisha: I'll also need to see a log sample that demonstrates redaction of raw prompts.
[09:24] Owen: We'll attach a log sample in the security packet.
[09:28] [09:35] Maya: Thanks everyone. Any final Qs?
[09:38] Tom: Just one — is there a way to tag requests for audit linking back to feature flags?
[09:44] Owen: Yes, we support request metadata tags. They show up in the audit UI and can be exported.
[09:49] Maya: Great. If nothing else, we'll wrap. Expect the security packet and benchmark plan in the next 2–3 business days.
[09:56] Daniel: Thanks, talk soon.
